item.title: How Gzip Makes the Web Feel Faster: Inside HTTP Compression
item.content:encoded:
Last week I was debugging a slow API and, out of habit, popped open Chrome DevTools and clicked the Network tab. Size and Transferred show up as two separate columns for every request there, and it’s easy to skim past a hundred times without noticing. This time I actually looked.

Size: 120 KB. Transferred: 32 KB.

My first thought was: did the browser skip loading part of the page? It hadn’t. Every div was in place, nothing missing. So where did the other 88 KB go?

Nothing got lost. The server packed the response into a smaller box before shipping it, and the browser unpacked it the moment it landed. That’s the whole trick behind why modern websites feel fast even when the page itself is huge. It’s called HTTP compression, and once you see how it works, you can’t un-see it in every Network tab you’ll ever open again.

Let’s walk through it the way a request actually travels.

Step 1: your browser announces what it can unwrap

Before your server sends back a single byte, your browser already told it something important, tucked into a header you’ve probably scrolled past a hundred times:

GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, zstd

That Accept-Encoding line is basically your browser leaning over and saying, "if you compress this, I know how to open it back up — gzip, Brotli, or Zstd, your call." This matters more than it looks. A server should never send a compressed file the client can't decompress. If the browser doesn't list an algorithm, the server just sends the plain, uncompressed version. No negotiation, no compression.

Here’s that negotiation as a sequence, since it’s really just two messages:

One request, one response, one header on each side. The browser proposes what it can handle, the server picks from that list, and it tells the browser exactly which one it used so decompression is unambiguous. No guessing on either end.

Step 2: your app has no idea any of this is happening

Here’s the part that surprised me the first time I actually thought about it: your Express route, your NestJS controller, your Django view — none of it knows compression exists. It builds a normal response. A string of HTML, a JSON object. That’s it. No .gz file, no compress() call, no awareness that any of this is going on.

Compression doesn’t happen inside your application. It happens around it, usually a couple of layers away from any code you’ll ever touch:

Browser
   │
   │  Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, zstd
   ▼
CDN / Reverse Proxy   ◄── compression usually happens here
   │
   │  (forwards the request, uncompressed)
   ▼
Your App (Express, Django, NestJS...)
   │
   │  returns a plain response — no idea compression exists
   ▼
CDN / Reverse Proxy   ◄── squeezes the response before sending it back
   │
   │  Content-Encoding: br
   ▼
Browser

Any layer between your app and the browser could be the one doing the actual squeezing — Nginx sitting in front of your app, Express’s compression middleware, or Cloudflare doing it at the edge before the request even reaches your origin. Doesn't matter which. Your application code stays exactly the same either way. It builds a response and hands it off; something else decides whether to shrink it.

Step 3: why does squeezing text even work?

This is the part that clicked for me once I stopped thinking of it as magic. Look at this chunk of HTML:

<div class="card">
<div class="card">
<div class="card">
<div class="card">

Same 18-ish characters, four times in a row. Instead of storing that phrase four separate times, a compression algorithm stores it once and leaves a note that says “copy the thing you saw a few lines up, again, right here.” Here’s roughly what that looks like once LZ77 gets through it:

BEFORE (36 bytes):
<div class="card">
<div class="card">
<div class="card">
<div class="card">

AFTER LZ77 (conceptually):
<div class="card">
[copy 19 bytes, back 19]
[copy 19 bytes, back 19]
[copy 19 bytes, back 19]

Multiply that across a full HTML document with repeated tags, repeated class names, repeated whitespace, and it’s easy to see why text shrinks so dramatically. Gzip stacks a second trick on top: Huffman coding, which gives the most common bytes shorter codes — the same idea as Morse code giving “E” a single dot because it shows up constantly in English.

Byte frequency in a typical HTML file:

'<'  ████████████████  very common  → short code   (e.g. 3 bits)
' '  ██████████████    very common  → short code   (e.g. 3 bits)
'e'  ██████████        common       → medium code  (e.g. 5 bits)
'z'  █                 rare         → long code    (e.g. 10 bits)

Repeated stuff is cheap. Unique stuff is expensive. That’s really the whole idea, and it’s a satisfying one once it clicks. HTML, CSS, JSON, and JavaScript are full of repetition, so they compress hard — usually 60 to 80 percent smaller.

Images are a different story. JPEG, PNG, and WebP already squeeze the redundancy out of the picture itself before the file is even saved to disk — that’s what makes them JPEG or PNG in the first place. By the time gzip gets to one of these files, there’s barely any repetition left to find. It’s like trying to pack a suitcase that’s already vacuum-sealed. Most servers just skip compressing images entirely and save the CPU.

Step 4: which algorithm actually wins

For a long time gzip was the only real option, and honestly it’s still fine. But two newer formats have mostly taken over for anything that cares about performance:

Gzip Brotli Zstandard Support basically everywhere nearly everywhere now newer, but growing fast Best at safe universal fallback pre-built static assets (your JS/CSS bundles) fast, high-volume dynamic responses CPU cost low to moderate can be heavy at max quality very cheap for what it gives you

Most production setups follow a simple ladder: try Brotli first if both sides support it, fall back to gzip, and if neither is supported, send the plain response. Nobody hand-picks the algorithm per request — the server works it out from the Accept-Encoding header on the fly.

That’s the entire decision tree a server walks through on every request. Nothing fancier than checking what the client claimed it could handle, in order of preference, and picking the first match.

The table above is accurate, but it’s worth seeing the actual trade-off as a shape rather than words. Roughly, for the same piece of text:

Output size after compression (smaller is better):

Gzip      ████████████████████████░░░░░░  ~70% of original
Brotli    ████████████████████░░░░░░░░░░  ~65% of original
Zstandard ████████████████████░░░░░░░░░░  ~66% of original
CPU cost to produce that output (smaller is better):
Gzip      ████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  low
Brotli    ████████████████████████░░░░░░  high at max quality
Zstandard ██████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  very low

Brotli usually wins on size, but it earns that by spending more CPU to find better compression opportunities. Zstandard’s whole pitch is the opposite trade: give up a little bit of size to get compression that’s cheap enough to run on every request without blinking. That’s why Brotli tends to win for static assets you compress once, and Zstandard is gaining ground for dynamic, high-traffic APIs.

Step 5: it costs CPU, so don’t max it out

Here’s a mistake I’ve actually made myself: cranking compression to the highest setting because smaller has to be better. It isn’t, not automatically. Every algorithm has a level dial — gzip runs 1 through 9, Brotli goes 0 through 11 — and the jump from level 6 to level 9 shaves off a little more size while costing a lot more CPU.

Compression level →   1 ─────── 6 ─────────── 9
File size saved   →   little    good           a little more
CPU time spent    →   little    moderate        a LOT more

For a static JS bundle you build once and cache forever, go ahead and max it out. You’re only paying that cost a single time. For a dynamic API response you’re generating fresh on every request, that math flips hard. Most production configs settle around gzip level 6 or Brotli quality 4–5 for exactly this reason.

The header everyone forgets, and the bug it causes

There’s one more header that quietly prevents a genuinely nasty bug:

Content-Encoding: br
Vary: Accept-Encoding

Picture a CDN sitting in front of your server. One visitor’s browser supports Brotli, gets a Brotli response, and the CDN caches it. A second visitor comes along whose browser only understands gzip. Without Vary: Accept-Encoding, the CDN has no idea it's not allowed to hand that cached Brotli response to a client that can't decode it — so it does anyway.

The second visitor’s browser gets a pile of bytes it can’t unpack, and the page shows up as garbled nonsense. It’s a one-line header, and it’s the difference between “compression saved us bandwidth” and “why is the site broken for some random subset of our users.” I didn’t even know this header existed until I got bitten by exactly this bug behind a CDN, and it took an embarrassingly long time to figure out why only some visitors saw a broken page.

What this actually saves you

Say an API returns 100 KB of JSON and gets hit a million times a day. Uncompressed, that’s 100 GB moving across the wire every day. Gzip it down to roughly 35 KB per response and you’re at 35 GB.

Daily bandwidth for one endpoint, 1M requests/day:

Uncompressed  ██████████████████████████████████████████  100 GB
Compressed    ███████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░   35 GB
                                                              ↑
                                                    65 GB saved, every day

That’s 65 GB saved, on one endpoint, every day. Multiply that across every page, every API call, every stylesheet a real site serves, and a handful of config lines end up being a meaningful chunk of a company’s actual cloud bill — not just a nice-to-have for page speed scores.

How does the browser know where the response ends?

Small detail, but people ask this a lot once they start digging. Every HTTP response usually carries a Content-Length header, and once compression kicks in, that number changes to match the compressed size, not the original one:

Content-Length: 32000

Not 120000. The browser reads that number, downloads exactly that many bytes, decompresses them, and knows it has the whole thing.

There’s a second way servers handle this, especially for APIs where the final size isn’t known upfront — think a response being streamed out piece by piece. Instead of Content-Length, you'll see:

Transfer-Encoding: chunked

That tells the browser “I don’t know the total size yet, I’ll send it in chunks and mark the end when I’m done.” You’ll run into this a lot on HTTP/1.1 APIs, and it works fine alongside compression too — the two aren’t in conflict, they just answer different questions.

The double-compression trap

Here’s one that’s bitten more teams than you’d think, including ones with solid engineers. Say your Express app compresses its own responses with the compression middleware. Then Nginx sits in front of it with gzip on in the config, doing the exact same job again.

Express (compress())  →  Nginx (gzip on)  →  Browser
        │                      │
   compresses once      tries to compress
   with gzip             an already-gzipped
                          body — wasted CPU,
                          or a broken response

Now you’re either compressing an already-compressed response a second time — which does almost nothing and just burns CPU on both layers — or worse, Nginx tries to gzip something that’s already gzipped and the browser ends up with a mess it can’t decode cleanly. The fix is boring: pick exactly one layer to own compression, usually the reverse proxy or CDN since it’s closer to the network, and turn it off everywhere else in the chain.

One security note: BREACH

This rarely makes it into beginner tutorials, but it’s worth knowing it exists. Back in 2013, researchers found an attack called BREACH that uses compression itself as a side channel — even over HTTPS. If a page reflects back something the attacker controls (like a search term) and a secret (like a CSRF token) in the same compressed response, an attacker can guess the secret one byte at a time. Guesses that partly match the real secret compress slightly smaller than ones that don’t, and that size difference leaks through, even encrypted.

You don’t need to memorize the mechanics. Just know the rule: don’t mix user-controlled input and secrets in the same compressed response, and if you’re not sure, that one endpoint is a fine place to just turn compression off.

The quick mistakes list

A few things worth double-checking if you’re setting this up yourself:

  • Don’t compress images, videos, or fonts that are already compressed — you’ll waste CPU for basically nothing.
  • Don’t max out the compression level for dynamic, per-request responses. Save max quality for stuff you build once, like static bundles.
  • Don’t forget Vary: Accept-Encoding if there's a CDN or any shared cache in front of your server.
  • Set a minimum size threshold, roughly 1 KB. Compressing a tiny 200-byte response can actually make it bigger once you add the compression overhead.
  • Pick exactly one layer in your stack to own compression. If your app and your reverse proxy are both compressing, turn one of them off.
  • Don’t reflect secrets and user-controlled input in the same compressed response — that’s the BREACH pattern from above.

Putting the whole request back together

That’s every piece. It’s worth seeing them in one place, because none of these steps is complicated on its own — the trick is that they all happen automatically, in order, without your application ever knowing:

Your browser asks what it can handle. Something in front of your app — never the app itself — picks an algorithm and squeezes the response. The response comes back labeled with exactly what was done to it, so decompression on the browser side is never a guess. Five steps, all of them boring, all of them the reason your Network tab shows a smaller number than the page actually contains.

The part users never see

None of this is visible to anyone using your site. Nobody’s ever going to open a support ticket that says “thanks for the Vary header." They just notice the page loaded fast and move on with their day. Which might be the actual point of most good infrastructure work — it disappears completely the moment it's done right, and the only proof it exists is a number in a Network tab that most people will never think to check.

How Gzip Makes the Web Feel Faster: Inside HTTP Compression was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Eliding Write Barriers: How .NET 10 Redefined Struct Returns for Performance
item.content:encoded:
Eliding Write Barriers: How .NET 10 Redefined Struct Returns for Performance

At first glance, new .NET releases might seem like just a series of version numbers and names.
But behind each version, changes happen that directly impact how fast your code runs without you having to change a single line.

One of the most interesting improvements in .NET 10 involves memory management and function calling conventions.
In previous .NET versions, when a function returned a large value like a struct with multiple fields, it had to allocate memory somewhere. Sometimes that was on the heap, sometimes on the stack.
This uncertainty meant the Garbage Collector (GC) had to get involved to track references and make sure nothing was accidentally collected.

From Write Barriers to Return Buffers

If you’ve been working with .NET for a while, you might look forward to tangible improvements whenever Microsoft releases a new runtime: new language features, LINQ enhancements, or API changes.
But a lot of real performance improvements happen where no one usually looks deep inside the GC and JIT compiler.

In .NET 10, several subtle changes in these components have made many applications run faster without a single line of your code changing.

What is a Write Barrier?

Imagine you create a new object and assign it to a field in your code:

person.Address = new Address(“123 Main St”);

On the surface, this looks like a simple assignment.
But behind the scenes, .NET has to ensure the GC is aware of this change.
The GC needs to know which objects point to which, so it doesn’t accidentally collect something still in use.

Every time a reference changes, the GC marks it, and this marking mechanism is called a Write Barrier.
Think of it like a control checkpoint that prevents memory chaos.

A simple analogy: imagine an office with a filing manager who needs to know where each file is stored.
If an employee moves a file and doesn’t inform the manager, chaos ensues when someone tries to find it.
The Write Barrier is like that phone call each employee makes to the manager after moving a file.

Why Write Barriers Can Be Costly

In most cases, the GC knows which parts of memory are short-lived (Gen0) and which are long-lived (Gen1 and Gen2).
The assumption is that most new objects are temporary.
So, for efficiency, the GC usually only scans Gen0 during minor collections.

But sometimes, a long-lived object (e.g., Gen2) references a short-lived object.
In this case, the GC must be aware of the reference; otherwise, it might collect the short-lived object too early.
This is exactly where Write Barriers come in.

Write Barriers are automatically inserted by the JIT compiler.
For every assignment that could cross generations, a call is added to the GC.
If your code has millions of assignments, these calls can become expensive.
In .NET 9, even when the GC didn’t really need to know, Write Barriers were still executed.
The JIT couldn’t always guarantee whether the reference lived on the heap or not, so it erred on the side of caution.

A Simple Example: Structs with Multiple Reference Fields

Consider this struct:

public record struct Person(string FirstName, string LastName, string Address, string City);

And a function that returns it:

public Person GetPerson()
 => new(_firstName, _lastName, _address, _city);

In .NET 9, each field Person would generate a Write Barrier — four calls to the GC for four simple fields.

What Changed in .NET 10?

In .NET 10, the runtime team made an important decision:

All return buffers must live on the stack, not on the heap.

But what is a return buffer?

When a function returns a Value Type (like a struct), the value needs to be stored somewhere until the caller can access it.
This storage space is called a Return Buffer.
In previous versions, the buffer could live on the heap, which meant GC tracking was necessary.
In .NET 10, the rule was standardized: return buffers always live on the stack.

Since the stack is outside the GC’s scope, no Write Barrier is needed when writing to it.

The Real-World Impact

As a result, when a function GetPerson executes, the JIT simply writes the values to the return buffer no GC calls required.

Practically, this means:

  • Short, frequent calls execute faster.
  • Code returning large data (like DTOs in APIs) can run tens of percent faster.
  • CPU usage decreases on heavy workloads.

In simple terms, .NET has learned when it doesn’t need to “call the GC.”

A Tangible Analogy

Imagine you work in an office where every time you create a new file, you have to report it to your manager.
In the old version, even if the manager knew the file was safely on your desk, you still had to notify them every time.
Now, in .NET 10, the manager is smarter: if the file is on your desk (the stack), no notification is needed.
Result? Work moves faster without any risk.

Changes on ARM64

Similar improvements occurred on ARM64 architecture.
Before .NET 10, all Write Barriers used a single universal model.
Now, a new system called WriteBarrierManager selects the appropriate barrier type based on GC state.

This change has two main benefits:

  1. Higher accuracy in identifying which memory regions actually need scanning.
  2. Reduced GC workload, since the entire memory space doesn’t need to be scanned unnecessarily.

In practice, this means your applications run faster on ARM devices, including servers like AWS Graviton or modern Macs, especially under heavy load.

Wrapping Up

At first glance, changes to Write Barriers or Return Buffers might seem minor.
But when repeated millions of times per second, their impact is remarkable.

These .NET 10 optimizations result in:

  • Hot paths executing up to 30% faster,
  • Reduced GC involvement,
  • More CPU time available for your actual code.

What’s happening here is a brilliant example of runtime intelligence in .NET:
changes that may be invisible at the code level, but are felt across the entire system.

In other words, speed often starts in the places no one sees, in the tiny details that only the runtime team considers.

Eliding Write Barriers: How .NET 10 Redefined Struct Returns for Performance was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Object Stack Allocation in .NET 10: A Deep Dive into Escape Analysis
item.content:encoded:
Object Stack Allocation in .NET 10: A Deep Dive into Escape Analysis

One of the most exciting advancements in deabstraction within .NET 10 is the broader use of escape analysis to enable stack allocation of objects.

In simple terms, stack allocation means that the JIT (Just-In-Time compiler) detects when an object (or array) is used only inside a method and does not “escape” beyond its scope. Instead of constructing the object on the heap, the JIT places it directly on the stack. This leads to less memory pressure, fewer GC operations, and much faster execution.
The Concept of Escape Analysis

Imagine the JIT evaluating where a newly created object should live:

  • On the heap: if the object might still be alive after the method returns.
  • On the stack: if the object’s lifetime is strictly confined to the current method and its call frame (i.e., no escape).

Escape Scenarios

The JIT must analyze whether an object escapes. Some dangerous cases include:

Returning an object

Foo MakeFoo() {
    return new Foo();
}

Here, the Foo An instance leaves the method; it must be on the heap.

Storing in a field or a static variable

class Bar { public Foo F; }
void Save(Bar b) {
    b.F = new Foo();
}

Here, the new Foo is stored inside another object → lifetime is unknown → must be on the heap.

Passing to an unknown method

void Print(object o) => Console.WriteLine(o);
void Test() {
    Print(new Foo());
}

Here, the JIT cannot be sure whether the object will be stored or retained; it must assume escape.

When Objects Don’t Escape

If the JIT determines the object is used only inside the method (not returned, not stored in a field, and not passed somewhere unsafe), it can be allocated on the stack:

void Test() {
 var foo = new Foo();
 foo.DoSomething();
}

Why Field-Sensitive and Inlining Matter

Field-Sensitive Analysis

The JIT needs to know if values inside a struct or Span trigger escape.

Span<int> s = stackalloc int[10];
s[0] = 42;

Safe: the data lives only within the stack frame.

Inlining

Inlining allows the JIT to see the flow of data. Without it, escape analysis might fail.

void Wrapper() {
    var f = MakeFoo();
    f.DoSomething();
}
Foo MakeFoo() => new Foo();

If MakeFoo is inlined, the JIT realizes the object never escapes → stack allocation becomes possible.

Escape Analysis on Delegates

Delegates are particularly interesting. Normally, invoking a delegate involves allocations:

public int Sum(int y)
{
    Func<int, int> addY = x => x + y;
    return DoubleResult(addY, y);
}

What Happens Under the Hood

  1. A closure object (display class) is created to capture y.
  2. A delegate object points to a method inside that closure.
    → Two allocations every time Sum it runs.

In .NET 9, this cost is unavoidable.
In .NET 10, the JIT is smarter:

  • It seems that the delegate is only passed to DoubleResult.
  • DoubleResult is inlined.
  • The JIT checks: “Is this delegate returned or stored anywhere?” No!

Result: the delegate allocation is eliminated. Only the closure remains.

Outcome:

  • Memory usage drops from ~88 bytes to ~24 bytes.
  • Performance nearly triples.

Explaining with an Analogy

  • .NET 9: You carry both a notebook (closure storing y) and a paper slip (delegate). Two items, two allocations.
  • .NET 10: The slip is unnecessary. You just use the notebook directly. One item, one allocation.

Escape Analysis on Arrays

Consider:

Process(new string[] { "a", "b", "c" });
  • The C# compiler allocates a string[] on the heap.
  • Even if Process doesn’t store or return it, allocation + GC overhead still occurs.

.NET 10 Scenario

The JIT checks:

  • Does this array escape? (return, field storage, unknown call?)
  • If not, it allocates the array on the stack transparently.

When the method ends, the stack frame is released; no GC pressure.

Analogy

  • .NET 9: You put words in a big cardboard box (heap), hand it over, and later throw it away (GC).
  • .NET 10: You lay the words directly on the table (stack): no box, no trash, no overhead.

Arrays and Span Example

private byte[] _buffer = new byte[3];

[Benchmark]
public void Test() => Copy3Bytes(0x12345678, _buffer);

[MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.NoInlining)]
private static void Copy3Bytes(int value, Span<byte> dest) =>
    BitConverter.GetBytes(value).AsSpan(0, 3).CopyTo(dest);

.NET 9 Behavior

  • BitConverter.GetBytes always allocates a 4-byte array on the heap.
  • Even though it’s immediately used and discarded, GC must still clean it.
  • Allocation cost: ~32 bytes.

.NET 10 Improvements

  • Inlining: GetBytes and AsSpan are inlined.
  • Escape analysis: JIT realizes the array is never returned or stored.

Result:

  • The 4-byte temporary lives on the stack.
  • No heap allocation.
  • No GC overhead.

The Big Picture

These optimizations are possible because of precise escape analysis combined with:

  • Field-sensitive tracking of structs and spans.
  • Inlining of small methods to expose usage patterns.
  • Understanding of low-level methods like Memmove to avoid false positives.

Analogy

Imagine splitting the number 0x12345678 into three bytes:

  • .NET 9: You build a 4-slot box on the heap, fill it, copy three slots, then throw the box away (GC cost).
  • .NET 10: You write the four values directly on the desk (stack), copy three, and wipe the desk clean when done.

Final Thoughts

The new escape analysis in .NET 10 represents a major leap forward. By reducing allocations, lowering GC pressure, and improving runtime performance, it makes .NET applications more efficient without requiring any changes from developers.

What once required manual tricks like stackalloc Now comes “for free” through smarter JIT analysis.

In short:

  • Less heap, more stack.
  • Fewer allocations, faster code.
  • A smarter runtime that gets out of your way.

With these optimizations, .NET 10 is shaping up to be one of the most performance-conscious releases in years.

Object Stack Allocation in .NET 10: A Deep Dive into Escape Analysis was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Optimizing Memory Management in .NET 9 with DATAS and VxSort
item.content:encoded:
Optimizing Memory Management in .NET 9 with DATAS and VxSort

Introduction: .NET 9 introduces significant enhancements to the garbage collection (GC) mechanism, particularly in the areas of memory management and fragmentation control. One of the most impactful features is DATAS (Dynamic Adaptation to Application Sizes), a new approach that dynamically adjusts heap size based on the volume of long-lived data in Gen 2 and the Large Object Heap (LOH). Additionally, the VxSort algorithm has been extended to Linux, bringing parallelized sorting to memory compaction processes. This article explores these optimizations in depth, demonstrating how they mitigate fragmentation and reduce GC pause times.

Understanding GC Heap Management in Previous .NET Versions: In previous .NET versions, GC primarily focused on managing new allocations and short-lived data in Gen 0 and Gen 1. However, long-lived data in Gen 2 was largely ignored in heap size calculations. This oversight led to scenarios where Gen 2 data accumulated without corresponding heap adjustments, increasing fragmentation and GC pause times.

Example Scenario: Consider an application that processes large datasets and caches significant amounts of data. Initially, data is allocated in Gen 0 and Gen 1. Over time, as objects survive multiple GC cycles, they are promoted to Gen 2. In previous .NET versions, despite this accumulation of long-lived data, GC would base heap size adjustments solely on the volume of new allocations, neglecting the persistent data in Gen 2.

The result? Excessive fragmentation and unpredictable memory usage, leading to longer GC pauses and increased working set sizes.

Introducing DATAS: Dynamic Adaptation to Application Sizes: DATAS addresses this oversight by continuously monitoring the volume of long-lived data in Gen 2 and LOH. Instead of focusing solely on new allocations, DATAS dynamically adjusts heap size based on the actual volume of live data. This adaptive strategy ensures that memory is efficiently allocated without excessive heap growth.

How DATAS Works:

  1. Continuous Monitoring: DATAS tracks the size of long-lived data in Gen 2 and LOH throughout the GC cycle.
  2. Dynamic Adjustment: If long-lived data grows, DATAS increases heap size appropriately to avoid unnecessary GC pauses.
  3. Compaction and Rearrangement: DATAS identifies opportunities to compact memory and rearrange objects to optimize locality and reduce fragmentation.

Example of DATAS in Action: Scenario: A web application processes large data batches periodically, with significant long-lived data retained in LOH. In previous .NET versions, this retained data would gradually fragment the heap, increasing GC pause times. With DATAS, the heap size adjusts dynamically, reducing fragmentation and optimizing memory allocation.

Bursty Workloads and Memory Management Challenges: Bursty workloads, characterized by rapid spikes in memory allocation followed by idle periods, pose unique challenges for GC. Examples include:

  • API servers processing large payloads intermittently.
  • Financial applications processing end-of-day transactions.
  • Messaging systems handling large batches of notifications.

DATAS addresses these challenges by actively monitoring memory usage patterns, ensuring that heap size is adjusted based on the actual volume of long-lived data rather than transient spikes.

Enhancements to Server GC in .NET 9: .NET 9 introduces several improvements to Server GC, particularly in how heap segments are allocated and managed. With DATAS enabled by default, the heap size is now more adaptive, preventing excessive memory consumption during low-activity periods while still accommodating bursty workloads efficiently.

VxSort: Optimized Parallel Sorting for Memory Compaction: Another key optimization in .NET 9 is the extension of the VxSort algorithm to Linux. Originally available only on Windows, VxSort leverages SIMD and parallel processing to reduce the time required for memory compaction.

Why VxSort?

  • SIMD Support: Enables simultaneous processing of multiple data elements, reducing sorting time.
  • Multi-Core Optimization: Distributes sorting workloads across multiple CPU cores.
  • Cache Efficiency: Minimizes cache misses during sorting, reducing overall GC latency.

Compacting the LOH: In previous versions, LOH compaction was either not prioritized or required explicit configuration. In .NET 9, LOH compaction strategies have been refined to reduce fragmentation. Developers can now trigger targeted compaction using

GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode=CompactOnce

Conclusion: The introduction of DATAS and the extension of VxSort to Linux represent significant advancements in memory management for .NET 9. By focusing on long-lived data and optimizing compaction through parallelized sorting, these features mitigate fragmentation, reduce GC pause times, and ensure more predictable memory usage across varied workloads.

Optimizing Memory Management in .NET 9 with DATAS and VxSort was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: The Story of My OpenAI .NET Contribution
item.content:encoded:
There is a particular kind of silence that surrounds you when you open a large codebase for the first time.

The repository is right there. The issue tracker is public. Every class, test, pull request, and design discussion is available to read. Nothing is technically preventing you from contributing.

And yet the distance between reading the code and changing the code feels enormous.

That was how I felt when I began working on the official [OpenAI .NET SDK](https://github.com/openai/openai-dotnet). The project is not a Microsoft-owned repository, but it sits deep inside the Microsoft .NET ecosystem: its public API conventions, dependency-injection experience, configuration model, and client architecture are closely connected to patterns used across .NET and the Azure SDK.

In other words, it was exactly the kind of codebase that could trigger imposter syndrome.

Who was I to propose a new dependency-injection experience for a library used by developers around the world? What if I had misunderstood the architecture? What if my pull request added noise instead of value? What if the maintainers looked at the implementation and immediately saw ten problems I had missed?

Those questions did not disappear before I started.

I started anyway.

What followed was not a quick open PR, receive approval, merge story. It became a journey of roughly five months from the first pull request on September 18, 2025, to the final merge on February 25, 2026. The code changed. The design changed. The scope expanded. The pull request was parked while a broader ecosystem design took shape. Then it came back to life, went through multiple rounds of review, crossed the last CI obstacles, and finally reached that small purple icon every contributor remembers.

This is the story of [pull request #696](https://github.com/openai/openai-dotnet/pull/696) and of how I learned that a successful open-source contribution is rarely just about writing the first version of the code.

The Problem Looked Simple At First

The developer experience I wanted to improve was familiar to almost every ASP.NET Core developer: registering OpenAI clients with the built-in dependency-injection container.

In an application, developers want client configuration to feel natural. They want to place settings in appsettings.json, override secrets through environment variables, register services during startup, and inject typed clients where they are needed.

A simplified version of the desired experience looked like this:

builder.AddChatClient("Chat");

public sealed class MyService(ChatClient chatClient)
{
    // Use chatClient...
}

The goal was easy to explain: make OpenAI clients fit naturally into the configuration and dependency-injection conventions .NET developers already understood.

But easy to explain is not the same as easy to design.

The first implementation approached the problem directly. My initial commit introduced IServiceCollection extension methods, an options type, support for configuration and environment variables, documentation, and unit tests. It was practical and recognizable to anyone who had built an ASP.NET Core integration.

I had done the work locally. I had read the surrounding code. I had added tests. I had written documentation. At some point, however, preparation stops being preparation. You have to put the work in front of other people.

I still remember the hesitation before clicking Create Pull Request.

The button itself is harmless. What it represents is not. It turns private reasoning into a public proposal. It says: I believe this belongs here.

Then I clicked it.

The First Review Was Bigger Than My Code

One of the first lessons arrived almost immediately: maintainers do not review a contribution only as a piece of working code. They review it as a permanent part of an ecosystem.

Stephen Toub raised a fundamental question: should this experience belong in the core SDK, or should it be handled by Aspire? Krzysztof Cwalina added that the configuration model needed to align with existing work across Aspire, .NET, and Azure. The concern was not that dependency injection was unimportant. It was that several teams were trying to solve related problems, and a local solution could accidentally create a new convention instead of joining a shared one.

That changed the nature of the discussion.

I had arrived with an implementation question: Does this code work?

The maintainers were asking an ecosystem question: Is this the right abstraction, in the right layer, using the right long-term pattern?

Those are very different questions.

For a contributor, this is a vulnerable moment. It is easy to translate architectural feedback into a personal verdict: My solution was rejected; therefore, I was not good enough. But that interpretation misses what maintainers are protecting. A widely used SDK pays for every public abstraction for years. Once an API ships, changing it is far more difficult than changing a pull request.

The feedback was not that you should not have tried. It was this idea touches a design larger than this repository.

On October 1, maintainer Jesse Squire explained that the team was still defining common patterns for client registration, construction, configuration, and alignment with the wider .NET ecosystem. Without a fully codified design, the team could not yet provide the detailed guidance needed to move the implementation forward. He offered three possibilities: close the pull request, revisit it later with a fresh implementation, or park it and collaborate after the design was ready.

I chose to park it.

That decision turned out to be one of the most important parts of the contribution.

I replied that I was happy to wait, iterate, and align the implementation with the broader patterns. [Michael Nash](https://github.com/m-nash) agreed that this was the best path and said we could collaborate when the design was ready.

For several months, the pull request remained open but intentionally paused.

At first, that felt like standing still. In retrospect, it was part of the work.

Open Source Also Means Knowing When to Wait

Developers are trained to value motion. We close tickets, push commits, reduce failing tests, and measure progress in visible changes. Waiting feels unproductive.

But mature open-source projects operate on a different scale. A contribution may depend on coordination between repositories, framework teams, design owners, release schedules, and API review processes. The best next action is sometimes not another commit. Sometimes it is preserving the conversation until the project is ready to make the right decision.

Parking the pull request taught me three things:

- A maintainer’s delay is not necessarily disinterest. It may reflect coordination that is invisible from the outside.

- Keeping a contribution alive does not mean repeatedly demanding attention. It means staying available, communicating respectfully, and being ready when the design becomes actionable.

- Code ownership and idea ownership are different. I had initiated the contribution, but the final design needed to belong to the project and its users — not to my first implementation.

That last point mattered most. If I had become emotionally attached to the original code, I would have defended the wrong thing. The goal was not to get my exact implementation merged. The goal was to improve the .NET developer experience in a way the maintainers could support for the long term.

The Pull Request Comes Back to Life

The turning point arrived with [issue #932: OpenAI: Add Configuration and DI Support](https://github.com/openai/openai-dotnet/issues/932).

The issue connected the OpenAI SDK work to the configuration and dependency-injection design in System.ClientModel. The accompanying [Azure SDK design documentation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-net/blob/main/sdk/core/System.ClientModel/src/docs/ConfigurationAndDependencyInjection.md) described a reusable model for configuration-bound client settings, normal and keyed DI registrations, credential resolution, nested client options, and shared configuration references.

This was the moment the architecture clicked for me.

The task was no longer adding some OpenAI-specific service-registration helpers. It was to translate a shared client-model pattern into the concrete structure of the OpenAI SDK.

That difference sounds subtle, but it changed almost everything.

The original implementation centered on direct IServiceCollection registration and an OpenAI-specific options object. The revised design centered on the following concepts:

- Each specialized client would receive its own strongly typed ClientSettings class.

- The properties of that settings class would mirror the parameters of the client’s primary constructor.

- Credential behavior would come from the shared base settings model instead of being reinvented in every derived type.

- Each client would gain a constructor that accepted its settings object.

- Registration would use IHostApplicationBuilder and the generic System.ClientModel infrastructure.

- Both ordinary and keyed registrations would be supported, allowing multiple differently configured clients of the same type.

For example, ChatClient had a main constructor shaped around a model, authentication policy, and client options. Therefore, its settings type needed to represent the configurable parts of that constructor:


[Experimental("SCME0002")]
public sealed class ChatClientSettings : ClientSettings
{
    public string? Model { get; set; }

    public OpenAIClientOptions? Options { get; set; }

    protected override void BindCore(IConfigurationSection section)
    {
        // Bind client-specific configuration.
    }
}

The corresponding constructor could then translate those settings into the client’s existing construction path:


[Experimental("SCME0002")]
public ChatClient(ChatClientSettings settings)
    : this(
        settings.Model,
        AuthenticationPolicy.Create(settings),
        settings.Options)
{
}

The exact implementation continued to evolve during review, but the architectural principle was now clear: settings should describe the client, while the shared client model should provide the common configuration and DI machinery.

This was my “Aha!” moment. I stopped seeing a collection of isolated extension methods and started seeing the SDK as one participant in a larger .NET client ecosystem.

Moving Fast and Discovering That the Design Was Still Moving

Once the direction was published, I moved quickly. Perhaps too quickly.

On February 5, I updated the pull request based on issue #932 and asked for review. Michael replied that I had started faster than he was ready; the issue did not yet contain every implementation detail. He updated it with the missing guidance.

That interaction captured something I grew to appreciate about the collaboration. The maintainer did not simply reject what was incomplete. He clarified the design, and I revised the implementation.

The relationship became less like submitter versus gatekeeper and more like two developers converging on a shared result.

By February 7, I had applied the additional details and returned the pull request for review. Then the real iteration began.

Trial by Fire: Learning Through Review

The review comments were detailed, but they were also remarkably instructive. Each one exposed a principle that extended beyond the line being discussed.

One Source of Validation Truth

In one client constructor, I had repeated parameter checks and fallback behavior that already existed in the primary constructor. Michael pointed out that the main constructor already owned this validation and that the new settings-based constructor should let it do its job.

The lesson was larger than removing a few lines:

Constructor overloads should converge on one validation path instead of creating parallel definitions of valid state.

Duplicated validation feels safe when you write it. Over time, however, it creates drift. One constructor accepts a value another rejects. One provides a default, another forgets. Centralizing construction rules makes behavior easier to reason about and maintain.

Configuration Names Are Part of the User’s Application

I had provided default configuration-section names for registration methods. The review challenged that assumption. A developer might need two chat clients, each with a different model, endpoint, or credential. The section could be called PrimaryChat, PremiumChat, or anything else meaningful to that application.

Removing the default was not merely an API-style preference. It preserved user choice and supported multi-client scenarios naturally.

That insight connected directly to keyed registration:


builder.AddKeyedChatClient("primary", "PrimaryChat");
builder.AddKeyedChatClient("premium", "PremiumChat");

The design was not just making one client easy to register. It was making an entire family of real deployment topologies possible.

Avoid Accidental Coupling

My revised implementation initially introduced a shared OpenAISpecializedClientSettings layer. It looked like a reasonable way to reduce repetition.

Michael suggested that every settings class inherit directly from ClientSettings because the extra OpenAI-specific layer would couple specialized clients more than necessary.

This was a valuable reminder: deduplication is not automatically good design. Sometimes a small amount of repeated structure is cheaper than a shared abstraction that forces unrelated types to evolve together.

Put Binding Logic Where the Data Is Understood

The configuration binding for OpenAIClientOptions initially lived outside the options type. The review moved that logic into an internal constructor on OpenAIClientOptions that accepted an IConfigurationSection.

Again, this was not just file organization. It placed interpretation next to the object that understood the meaning and validation of those values.

Completeness Is Part of Consistency

My first pass covered the obvious specialized clients: chat, embeddings, audio, images, and moderation. Then the review pointed out that the SDK contained many more client types: assistants, batches, containers, conversations, evaluation, files, fine-tuning, graders, real-time, responses, vector stores, videos, and others.

If the feature shipped for only a visible subset, developers would encounter an inconsistent SDK: one client could be configured through the new pattern while another still required manual construction.

So the scope expanded.

By the final version, the pull request touched more than forty files, including API-surface listings, settings classes, client constructors, host-builder extensions, option binding, and dedicated tests. What began as a handful of DI helpers had become a systematic capability across the client family.

That expansion was not scope creep. It was the natural consequence of understanding the architecture correctly.

The Moment the Feedback Changed Tone

There is a subtle but unmistakable moment in a long review when the conversation changes.

At first, comments challenge the shape of the design. Later, they refine details. The questions move from should this abstraction exist? to can we make this expression more explicit? And could these methods be ordered alphabetically?

On February 10, after the architectural changes had landed, Michael wrote that there was one minor update left and that the work was looking good.

Two days later, his review said: “Changes LGTM, thanks again.”

For a contributor, those few words carry surprising weight. They do not mean the work is finished, but they mean the core idea has crossed an important boundary. The code is no longer being evaluated as an external proposal. It is beginning to look like part of the project.

Then another review arrived.

Copilot identified missing null checks across the new settings-based constructors and asked for test coverage around configuration binding, ordinary registrations, and keyed registrations. José Harriaga reviewed those findings and proposed removing constructor chaining in places where explicit validation and initialization would produce a clearer, safer construction path. He also asked for registration methods to be ordered consistently so future maintainers could more easily identify missing clients.

The pull request moved back into a changes-requested state.

Earlier in the journey, that might have felt like losing ground. By then, I understood it differently. An approval is not a finish line if another reviewer finds a real gap. The code had improved enough to invite a deeper level of scrutiny.

I applied the requested changes and thanked José for the thorough review.

The Last Mile Was Not Glamorous

The final stretch of an open-source contribution is often less cinematic than the architecture work.

There were generated API listings to update. There was a repository script, Export-Api.ps1, that needed to be run. CI still failed after I believed the API files were current. There were follow-up branches and maintainer pull requests to reconcile. There was another request to regenerate the API surface. I ran the script again, but it produced no changes. Michael helped bridge the remaining repository-state issues through small pull requests against my fork.

This part of the story matters because production-quality contribution is not only the elegant design discussion. It is also:

- understanding project-specific build scripts;

- keeping generated public API files synchronized;

- responding clearly when local results and CI results disagree;

- accepting help when maintainers can resolve a repository-specific problem faster;

- and staying engaged after the interesting coding work is complete.

On February 25, Michael approved the pull request and asked José for one last look. José approved it at 09:01 UTC.

One minute later, [pull request #696 was merged](https://github.com/openai/openai-dotnet/pull/696).

The Purple Badge

GitHub represents a merged pull request with a small purple icon.

Visually, it is almost nothing.

Emotionally, it contains the entire journey.

It contains the anxiety before the first submission. The early architectural questions. The moment the pull request was blocked to prevent an accidental merge. The choice to park the work instead of abandoning it. The months of waiting. The new design issue. The rewrite. The detailed review from Michael. The broader review from José. The failing CI. The generated API files. The final approvals.

Most importantly, it contains a change in perspective.

When I opened the pull request, I thought success meant proving that my initial solution was good enough.

When it merged, I understood that success meant helping the project arrive at the right solution even when that required replacing much of my first approach.

The Ripple Effect: A Contribution Larger Than One Convenience Method

The final feature was not an isolated OpenAI-specific DI shortcut. It implemented a pattern connected to System.ClientModel, the shared client infrastructure documented in the Azure SDK repository.

That broader design supports capabilities such as:

- strongly typed settings loaded from configuration;

- nested pipeline, retry, endpoint, logging, and client options;

- credentials supplied through configuration or external resolvers;

- ordinary and keyed client registrations;

- multiple instances of the same client type;

- and reference syntax for sharing configuration across clients.

The ripple effect therefore ran in both directions. The wider .NET and Azure SDK design reshaped my pull request, and the OpenAI .NET SDK became a concrete adopter of that design across its specialized clients.

That is a more meaningful outcome than adding a few helper methods. It creates consistency. A .NET developer who learns the pattern in one client library can recognize it elsewhere. Maintainers gain a common model. Future client types have a clear extension path.

The experience changed how I think about architecture: sometimes the most valuable contribution is not inventing a unique abstraction. It is recognizing the shared abstraction and implementing it faithfully in a new context.

Technical Takeaways I Will Carry Forward

The review produced several lessons I now treat as reusable engineering principles:

- Design the public API for the ecosystem, not only the immediate example. A registration method that works for one default client may fail when an application needs several differently configured instances.

- Route overloads through a single construction and validation model. Duplicating validation across constructors creates subtle inconsistencies.

- Do not introduce inheritance only to remove repetition. A shared base type can become unwanted coupling between otherwise independent clients.

- Place binding logic close to the type that owns the meaning of the values. Configuration parsing, defaults, and validation should not be scattered across unrelated extension classes.

- Consistency requires complete coverage. If a feature applies conceptually to a family of clients, partial implementation can create a confusing public surface.

- Keyed DI is not an edge case. Multiple models, endpoints, tenants, or credentials are normal production requirements.

- Tests must verify the developer experience, not merely registrations. It is not enough to see a service descriptor in the container; configuration binding and resolved clients must behave correctly.

- Generated API artifacts are part of the contract. Public API baselines and export scripts deserve the same attention as handwritten code.

What I Learned About Communication

The technical lessons were only half of it.

The contribution also taught me that communication is part of implementation.

I learned to ask for status without assuming neglect. I learned to distinguish a blocked design from a rejected contributor. I learned to state clearly when changes were ready, summarize what I had run, and describe what remained broken. I learned that a short response such as I’m happy to iterate when the design is ready can preserve months of future collaboration.

Good open-source communication is neither passive nor demanding. It is precise, patient, and oriented toward shared ownership.

The best exchanges in the pull request were not transactions where a maintainer issued instructions and I followed them. They were moments of collaborative reasoning:

The shared base class may reduce repetition, but will it couple the clients?

The constructor can validate here, but is that already the responsibility of the main constructor?

A default section name is convenient, but what happens when the user needs two chat clients?

The obvious clients are covered, but what will the SDK feel like when a developer reaches a less common one?

Those questions made the implementation better, but they also made me a better engineer.

Advice for Developers Making Their First Major Contribution

If you are staring at a large repository and wondering whether you belong there, here is what I would tell you now:

1. Start before the imposter syndrome disappears

Confidence often arrives after action, not before it. Read the code, narrow the problem, add tests, and make the proposal.

2. Treat your first implementation as a conversation starter

The code gives maintainers something concrete to evaluate. Its value does not disappear if the architecture changes.

3. Separate feedback about the design from judgment about yourself

A strong reviewer may challenge the foundation of your approach. That is not the same as challenging your right to contribute.

4. Optimize for the merged solution, not for preserving your original code

Deleting or rewriting your own work is not failure. It is often evidence that you understand the problem more deeply than when you began.

5. Learn the repository’s operational rituals

Formatting, generated files, API baselines, test conventions, and CI scripts are part of the project’s engineering culture.

6. Be patient without disappearing

If a design is blocked, agree on the next step, remain available, and return when the project has enough clarity to proceed.

7. Notice when collaboration begins

The moment a maintainer starts explaining trade-offs, proposing concrete alternatives, or helping repair the last CI issue, you are no longer simply asking for acceptance. You are building something together.

Final Reflection

My pull request began with a practical idea: make OpenAI clients easier to configure and inject in .NET applications.

It ended as something much more valuable.

I learned how a mature SDK evaluates public API design. I learned why ecosystem alignment can matter more than a locally elegant solution. I learned that waiting can be an engineering decision. I learned that review comments are often compressed architecture lessons. I learned that completeness, tests, generated API files, and CI are all part of shipping — not administrative work surrounding it.

And I learned that open source is not a stage on which a contributor proves individual brilliance.

At its best, it is a place where people with different context gradually build a shared understanding. The contributor brings energy, time, and a concrete proposal. Maintainers bring historical knowledge, ecosystem constraints, and responsibility for the future. Review turns those inputs into something neither side would have produced alone.

The purple Merged badge was satisfying. Of course it was.

But the deeper victory was realizing that I could enter a codebase that initially intimidated me, stay through uncertainty and revision, learn from people who understood the ecosystem at a different depth, and help carry a feature all the way into the project.

The first commit mattered because it began the journey.

The merge mattered because I did not insist that the journey end where I first imagined it would.

item.title: Read-Modify-Write isolation in NoSQL, part 2: When the invariant spans multiple aggregates.
item.content:encoded:
In part 1 we saw the single-document case, where optimistic locking saves you with a simple version field. Now we cross the line that breaks that comfort.

Let me make it concrete. Your product sells seats, and an organization buys a license capped at 100 seats. Those seats are spread across many Teams, and each Team is its own aggregate with its own lifecycle. You can’t stuff the list of all teams into one document: it grows unbounded and violates every aggregate-design instinct you have.

So your invariant is a sum across aggregates:

The sum of seats over all Team aggregates must never exceed 100.

To enforce that on every “add seats to a team” operation, the honest move is to read the current state across every Team and sum it — a fan-out that scans N Team documents and gets slower as the org grows. Painful, yes. But surely reading the real, current teams inside a transaction is at least correct? That intuition is the trap.

Now the operation is a textbook Read → Modify → Write — but watch what each step touches. You read and sum the Team documents as your guard, confirm there’s room, then write the 8 seats onto one Team aggregate (Team Alpha, Team Beta — each its own document). The check reads a set of documents; the mutation lands on one of them. And that's where it gets dangerous.

The anomaly: Write Skew

Two requests run concurrently. The teams currently sum to 90.

guard: Σ seats over all Team docs = 90   (max 100)
  Tx A   reads all teams → Σ = 90 → 90+8 ≤ 100 ✅ → writes Team Alpha (+8) → COMMIT
  Tx B   reads all teams → Σ = 90 → 90+8 ≤ 100 ✅ → writes Team Beta  (+8) → COMMIT
         └─ each reads its OWN snapshot — neither sees the other's in-flight
            write. Two DIFFERENT Team docs → no write-write conflict to abort.
  Σ seats across Team aggregates = 106   >   license cap 100
  Nothing collided, nothing was overwritten.
  The invariant dies between the documents. That's Write Skew.

Each transaction read a valid state and made a locally correct decision — yet the real total is now 106, and you've oversold a 100-seat license. The subtle part the trace makes visible: the damage isn't an overwrite. It lives between the documents, because both transactions validated against a 90 that didn't yet include the other's write.

This is Write Skew, and it’s exactly where naive optimistic locking gives up. You’d put a version on the Team document — but Alpha and Beta were never contended; they're different documents. The contended truth is the seat invariant itself.

💡 Lost update vs. Write Skew — the line this whole series turns on.
Part 1’s bug was an overwrite: two writes hit the same document, one erased the other, and the stored value itself came out wrong (10 instead of 11). This is the opposite. Nothing is overwritten — the two writes land on different documents, both commit cleanly, and every document stays internally consistent. The invariant breaks in the gap between them. Same Read → Modify → Write race, a strictly nastier failure: there’s no torn document for a code review, a unit test, or the database to catch.

A precise word on isolation levels

Wrap the whole thing in a native MongoDB multi-document transaction (≥ 4.0 on replica sets, 4.2+ on sharded clusters) and you get snapshot isolation: every transaction sees a consistent point-in-time snapshot of the database. That genuinely eliminates the classic ANSI read anomalies — dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and even phantoms (the snapshot is frozen, so rows born after it are simply invisible) — plus single-document lost updates.

What it does not give you, on its own, is full serializability — so it can’t stop Write Skew. The subtle part most people miss: your clean snapshot isn’t enough, because the concurrent transaction is reading its own snapshot — stale relative to yours — and writing based on it. Two consistent snapshots, two valid decisions, one broken invariant.

Here’s the mental key most devs skip: the invariant is never encoded as a write conflict. WiredTiger (MongoDB’s storage engine) only aborts a transaction when two of them write the same document. Tx A wrote Team Alpha, Tx B wrote Team Beta — different documents, so there's nothing for WiredTiger to abort. The constraint lives in your head and your validation check, not in the data the engine is watching for conflicts. Snapshot isolation protects the bytes; it can't protect a rule it was never told about.

So the fix — whatever you reach for — has to do the one thing the engine never did for you: make the invariant part of what it watches for conflicts. And here’s the uncomfortable preview of everything that follows: every way of doing that ends up serializing these writes somehow, and every one sends you a bill.

the rule    Σ(team.seats) ≤ 100              ← the engine never watches this
the move    materialize it into one doc every writer must also touch:
            license = { usedSeats: 90, maxSeats: 100 }
            → the invisible skew becomes a write-write conflict it CAN catch
              (doing it right — and what it costs — is the rest of this series)

The pattern underneath

Strip it back and the lesson is one sentence. Write skew isn’t a flaw in transactions, and MongoDB isn’t “wrong.” Write skew is what happens when an invariant never becomes part of the database’s conflict-detection model — a mismatch between the scope you validate (all the Team docs) and the scope the engine watches for conflicts (the one doc you write). The same read scope ≠ write scope gap from the guard above, all the way up.

Hold that sentence — it’s the lens for everything that follows. Every cure from here is just a different answer to one question: how do I drag the invariant into something that serializes these writes? And not one of them is free.

Where this leads

So we reach for the reflex everyone tries first: a distributed lock. Freeze the world around the read and the write with Redis, and on paper you’re finally serializable. In practice it’s a minefield — latency, deadlocks, and a TTL dilemma with no good answer.

That’s where things get ugly. Part 3.
